topics.title: 16.1 cmp
topics.summary: cmp source, destination sets flags as though it computed destination minus source, but discards the arithmetic result. In AT&T syntax, cmpq %rsi, %rdi therefore compares %rdi against %rsi . The following branch determines whether the comparison is interpreted as signed or unsigned. The cmp instruction itself does not carry a high-level signedness tag. A wrong branch condition can make identical input patterns produce an incorrect ordering even though the subtraction flags were generated correctly.

topics.title: 16.2 test
topics.summary: test sets flags from a bitwise AND without storing the AND result. testq %rax, %rax is a common way to test whether a register is zero. test with a mask checks selected bits. Testing a value against itself also exposes its sign bit through the sign flag, but the intended predicate must still be clear. A masked test followed by a zero branch means no selected bit was set. It does not mean all unselected bits were zero or that the entire value equals the mask.

topics.title: 16.3 Condition flags
topics.summary: For common comparisons, zero ( ZF ) indicates equality, sign ( SF ) reflects the result’s sign bit, carry ( CF ) supports unsigned order, and overflow ( OF ) corrects signed-order interpretation when subtraction’s sign alone would mislead. A useful subset is: Keep the comparison and branch adjacent in your reasoning even when scheduling places other instructions between them. An instruction that changes relevant flags changes the branch’s input.

topics.title: 16.4 Conditional branches
topics.summary: A conditional branch transfers control when a flag predicate is true. Otherwise execution continues with the following instruction. The processor may predict the outcome and execute speculatively, but architectural behavior must match the permitted branch result. A misprediction can waste speculative work, yet removing a branch is not automatically faster. A branch may avoid an expensive or invalid operation. A branchless replacement that computes both alternatives can increase work or access memory that the original branch protected. Preserve semantics before comparing speed.

topics.title: 16.5 Unconditional branches
topics.summary: An unconditional jump changes the next instruction without testing flags. It can target a fixed label or an address obtained indirectly. Compilers use jumps to connect basic blocks, implement loop back edges, and skip alternate paths. An indirect jump’s target must be valid for the intended control-flow graph. Table indices and function pointers need bounds and type validation. A control-flow error can redirect execution even when no arithmetic result is wrong. Security mechanisms can constrain some targets, but the program must still maintain valid dispatch state.

topics.title: 16.6 Loops
topics.summary: A loop usually contains initialization, a condition, a body, an update, and a back edge. Compilers may place the condition at the top or bottom, duplicate a test, or transform the induction variable. The resulting assembly can look different from the source while preserving the iteration domain. To understand a loop, identify its invariant and progress measure. A pointer may advance while a count decreases. An index may be compared against an end value. Determine whether the loop handles zero iterations before examining the body; many off-by-one errors arise from assuming at least one element exists.

topics.title: 16.7 Conditional moves
topics.summary: A conditional move selects a value according to flags without a control-flow branch. It can be effective when both candidate values are cheap and valid to compute. Do not use it to hide an invalid address behind a false condition. High-level conditional expressions also have language evaluation rules that the compiler must preserve for valid programs.

topics.title: 16.8 Jump tables
topics.summary: A jump table stores branch targets or offsets indexed by a selector. It can efficiently dispatch among many dense cases. The compiler normally includes a range check before indexing the table, possibly after subtracting the lowest case value. Sparse selectors may be better served by comparisons or a search structure. A table’s size and locality also matter. The fact that a source switch has many cases does not guarantee a jump table, and the presence of a table does not mean every possible input is a valid index.

topics.title: 16.9 switch translation
topics.summary: A switch can become a jump table, comparison tree, sequence of branches, arithmetic transformation, or data lookup. Cases returning constants may become a value table rather than a table of instruction addresses. Optimization depends on case density and behavior. When inspecting translation, start with the source’s semantic mapping from input values to outcomes. Then identify how the assembly implements that mapping and handles the default case. This avoids mistaking a compact arithmetic transformation for missing cases or assuming a table entry is executable code when it is merely data.

topics.title: Worked example — A count-controlled sum loop
topics.summary: The requirement is to sum a valid array of 64-bit unsigned values, with modular 64-bit addition. A zero-length input must return zero without reading memory.
